name: Spanish Empire
tierReason: American silver makes you rich fast, but costly wars and debt can sink you.
summary: Fund Columbus, build an empire in the Americas, and decide what to do with a mountain of silver.
intro: You begin as Queen Isabella in 1492 and guide the Spanish Crown through Charles V, Philip II, and their heirs. Your strengths: daring explorers, conquests in the Americas, and more silver than any empire before you. Your challenges: enemies across Europe, the Protestant Reformation, rebellions, and the temptation to spend your fortune on endless wars.

collapse.text: Endless wars and unpaid debts bankrupted the Crown. Your armies mutinied, provinces broke away, and the Spanish Empire fell apart.

survive.text: Your Spanish Empire still stretches from Mexico to Peru to the Philippines in 1750.

glossary.def: the centuries-long Christian campaign to retake Spain from Muslim rulers

timeline.text: Spain conquers Granada, expels Jews who refuse to convert, and funds Columbus's first voyage.
Conquistadors, helped by Indigenous allies and smallpox, conquer the Aztec and Inca empires.
Silver is found at Potosí. From the 1570s, the mita forced-labor system sends Indigenous workers into its mines.
The northern Netherlands, led by Protestants, revolt against Spain and in 1648 finally win independence.
The Spanish Armada fails to invade England.

The last Spanish Habsburg king dies in 1700, leaving Spain to a French Bourbon, Philip V. He keeps the throne after the War of the Spanish Succession, but Spain loses its lands in Italy and the Netherlands.

columbus.title: A Sailor's Wild Idea
columbus.text: You are Queen Isabella of Castile, ruling Spain with your husband, King Ferdinand of Aragon. In January 1492 your armies captured Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, completing the Reconquista. Now an Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus asks you to pay for a voyage west across the Atlantic to reach Asia. Your experts say he has badly underestimated the size of the Earth, and they're right.

scene.title: A new world
scene.caption: Granada falls in January 1492. In August Columbus sails west, and in October he lands in the Bahamas, opening the Americas to Spain.

options.text: Pay for the voyage. It's a cheap gamble on reaching Asia's riches before Portugal does.
options.explanation: A cheap bet that changed history. Columbus never reached Asia (he landed in the Bahamas and the Caribbean in October 1492), but his voyages opened the Americas to Spanish conquest. Within a century, American silver helped make Spain the most powerful empire in Europe.

options.text: Refuse. Your experts have checked his numbers, and Asia is far too distant to reach by sailing west. His crews would run out of food and water long before land, and your money would be lost.
options.explanation: The experts were right about the distance, but nobody in Europe knew two continents lay in the way. Isabella and Ferdinand funded Columbus, and his 1492 landing in the Caribbean began Spain's empire in the Americas.

options.text: Skip the voyage and focus on forcing Spain's Jews and Muslims to convert or leave, so Spain becomes entirely Catholic.
options.explanation: In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella really did order Spain's Jews to convert or leave, and the Inquisition hunted suspected heretics. Spain lost many skilled merchants and craftspeople, but the rulers also funded Columbus, a far better investment.

tordesillas.title: Dividing the World
tordesillas.text: Columbus has returned with gold, parrots, and captured Taíno people, claiming he reached Asia. Portugal, which has been exploring Africa's coast, is furious and says the new lands belong to it. War between the two Catholic kingdoms looks possible.

options.text: Negotiate with Portugal and draw a line down the Atlantic: lands to the west for Spain, lands to the east for Portugal.
options.explanation: That's the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494). The Pope had drawn a first line in 1493, but the two kingdoms negotiated their own line farther west. It avoided war and gave Spain most of the Americas, while Portugal got Africa, the sea route to India, and later Brazil.

options.text: Go to war with Portugal over the new lands. Columbus found them sailing under your flag, and if you let Portugal bully you now, it will try to grab every discovery that follows.
options.explanation: A war between Europe's two leading sea powers would waste the fleets both needed. Instead, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494, splitting the lands beyond Europe between them.

options.text: Keep the new lands secret and tell the other kingdoms nothing.
options.explanation: News of Columbus's voyage was already spreading across Europe. Spain secured its claim openly through the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).

second_chance.title: Rivals at Sea
second_chance.text: Portugal has reached India by sailing around Africa (1498), and its ships return loaded with spices. Meanwhile, sailors report vast, unknown lands across the Atlantic. Your advisers warn that Spain is falling behind its rival.

options.text: Fund more expeditions across the Atlantic and claim the new lands for Spain. Use the Caribbean islands as bases, and explore the mainland before any rival gets there.
options.explanation: Better late than never. In reality, Spain had funded Columbus back in 1492, and by 1500 Spanish settlements were growing in the Caribbean. Those islands became the base for Spain's conquests on the mainland, starting with the Aztec Empire.

options.text: Send your own fleets around Africa to India to compete with Portugal.
options.explanation: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) had already given that route to Portugal, so this would mean war. Spain's future lay west, in the Americas.

options.text: Give up on overseas exploration and focus on the wars in Italy. Rich lands close to home are worth more than distant islands no one has mapped.
options.explanation: Spain did fight in Italy, but giving up on the Americas would mean giving up the silver that later paid for everything. Spain's American colonies became the foundation of its empire.

aztecs.title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
aztecs.text: You are now King Charles I of Spain, Isabella's grandson, who since 1519 has also ruled the Holy Roman Empire as Charles V. The conquistador Hernán Cortés, with about a thousand Spaniards, tens of thousands of Indigenous allies who hated Aztec rule, and the help of a terrible smallpox epidemic, has captured the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan. Cortés wants to rule Mexico himself, and his men want land and native laborers as rewards.

scene.title: Viceroys, not conquistadors
scene.caption: Tenochtitlan falls in 1521, and Mexico City rises on its ruins. Spain rules through the Council of the Indies (1524) and viceroys of New Spain (1535) and Peru (1540s).

options.text: Take power from the conquistadors: create a Council of the Indies in Spain and set up viceroyalties run by royal appointees.
options.explanation: Smart, and historical. The Council of the Indies (1524) and viceroys in New Spain (1535) and Peru (1540s) kept the colonies under royal control. Conquistadors won glory, but the Crown kept the power.

options.text: Let Cortés and the conquistadors rule as lords of the lands they conquered. They risked their lives, they know the country, and governing it from across an ocean would be slow and costly.
options.explanation: Dangerous: conquistadors far from Spain could become independent kings. In Peru, Gonzalo Pizarro's followers actually rebelled against royal rule in the 1540s, and the Crown fought hard to keep control.

options.text: Reward the conquistadors with encomiendas, but keep a royal governor in charge.
options.explanation: This is close to what happened at first. But the encomienda system led to terrible abuse of Indigenous people, whose populations were also devastated by disease, and the settlers who held encomiendas grew powerful enough to challenge the Crown.

council.title: The New Laws
council.text: Reports from the Americas are horrifying. Under the encomienda system, Spanish settlers force Indigenous people to work in mines and fields. Millions have died, mostly from diseases like smallpox but also from overwork and violence. A priest named Bartolomé de las Casas begs you to protect them. The settlers say the colonies will collapse without forced labor.

options.text: Pass laws banning Indigenous slavery and phasing out the encomienda, but soften them if settlers revolt.
options.explanation: Close to what Charles did with the New Laws of 1542. Settlers in Peru revolted, so the Crown softened the laws, but they still weakened the encomienda holders and strengthened royal control. Forced labor continued, though, through other systems like the mita.

options.text: Ignore Las Casas. The settlers warn that the colonies will collapse without forced labor, and the profits matter more than one priest's complaints.
options.explanation: Letting settlers do whatever they wanted would create powerful, abusive colonial lords who answered to no one. The Crown passed the New Laws in 1542 to limit the encomienda and assert royal authority.

options.text: Abolish all forced labor immediately and punish any settler who resists. Half-measures will only let the abuse go on, and the Crown must show it means what it says.
options.explanation: Morally appealing, but in 1542 the settlers would have rebelled, as they did in Peru even against the milder New Laws. The Crown chose partial limits and kept forced labor in other forms, like the mita.

conquistadors.title: Rebellion in Peru
conquistadors.text: In Peru, conquered from the Inca by Francisco Pizarro in the 1530s, Spanish settlers grew rich and powerful on native labor. When you try to limit their power, Pizarro's brother Gonzalo leads a rebellion, kills your viceroy in battle, and talks of becoming king of Peru himself.

options.text: Send a skilled royal negotiator to Peru. Offer pardons to rebels who switch sides and soften the laws that angered them, so Gonzalo Pizarro is left with few followers.
options.explanation: That's what worked. The royal envoy Pedro de la Gasca won over most of Gonzalo Pizarro's followers with pardons, and Pizarro was defeated and executed in 1548. Royal control over Peru was restored.

options.text: Let Gonzalo Pizarro rule Peru, as long as he sends you silver. Fighting him from across an ocean could cost far more.
options.explanation: Giving in to a rebel would invite every colony to break away. The Crown sent Pedro de la Gasca, who defeated Pizarro in 1548 and restored royal control.

options.text: Send a huge army across the ocean to crush the rebels.
options.explanation: Possible, but slow and very expensive, since Peru was months away by sea. The Crown won more cheaply with pardons and diplomacy, and Pizarro was defeated in 1548.

silver.title: Mountains of Silver
silver.text: You are now King Philip II. In 1545 a mountain of silver was found at Potosí, high in the Andes. Soon a forced labor draft called the mita will send thousands of Indigenous workers into its mines, and Spain will mine more silver than any empire before it. Treasure fleets carry it to Spain, and Manila galleons carry it across the Pacific, where Chinese merchants trade silk and porcelain for it. But you have also inherited huge debts and wars against France and the Ottomans, while Protestantism spreads across Europe.

scene.title: Silver in, silver out
scene.caption: Silver from Potosí crosses the ocean in treasure fleets, but much of it flows straight out again to pay for wars and foreign goods. The Crown goes bankrupt several times.

context.text: Royal officials, not conquistadors, run your American colonies, so the silver flows to the Crown.

options.text: Use the silver to pay off debts, build up Spain's own farms and workshops, and avoid needless wars.
options.explanation: The road not taken. Philip and his heirs spent the Crown's silver and Castile's taxes on wars, and much private silver bought goods made abroad, so Spain went bankrupt several times and its wealth flowed to other countries. The flood of silver also helped cause inflation across Europe.

options.text: Spend it on armies and fleets to defend Catholicism everywhere: against Protestants, the Ottomans, and France. As Europe's leading Catholic monarch, it is your sacred duty, and now you finally have the money.
options.explanation: This is close to what Philip II did. Endless wars cost more than even American silver could pay for, and Spain's government stopped paying its debts in 1557, 1560, 1575, and 1596.

options.text: Spend it on luxuries and goods imported from abroad. Spain is rich now, and foreign workshops already make what you need, so why build your own?
options.explanation: Much of Spain's silver really did flow out to pay for foreign goods and loans, enriching Dutch, Italian, and German merchants and bankers, while Spain's own industries fell behind.

dutch.title: Trouble in the Netherlands
dutch.text: You rule the Netherlands, a rich land of merchants and cloth makers. Many Dutch have become Protestants since the Protestant Reformation began. As Europe's leading Catholic monarch, you have enforced harsh laws against heretics, and in 1566 Protestant crowds smash statues in Catholic churches. Dutch nobles beg you to ease up.

options.text: Ease the harsh laws against Protestants, keep local Dutch nobles in charge, and avoid a long war.
options.explanation: The road not taken. Philip sent the Duke of Alba with an army and executed many rebels, and the Dutch Revolt that followed lasted 80 years (1568–1648), cost Spain a fortune, and ended with independence for the northern Netherlands.

options.text: Send your toughest general and an army to crush the Protestant rebels.
options.explanation: This is what Philip did in 1567. The Duke of Alba's harsh crackdown turned unrest into a full revolt that drained Spain for 80 years and ended with an independent Dutch Republic, a Protestant trading rival.

options.text: Let church courts quietly put heretics on trial, without sending an army. The law stays firm, the Protestants are punished, and you avoid the huge cost of a war far from Spain.
options.explanation: Harsh heresy trials, and fears that Philip would bring in the Spanish Inquisition, were part of what angered the Dutch in the first place. Philip sent an army in 1567, and the revolt lasted until 1648.

bankrupt.title: The King Is Broke
bankrupt.text: Despite all the American silver, Spain cannot pay its debts. In 1575 your government stops paying its bankers, again. In the Netherlands, where rebels have been fighting since 1568, your unpaid soldiers are close to mutiny.

options.text: Cut back: make peace wherever you can, pay your soldiers first so they stay loyal, and reform taxes so the nobles finally pay their share of the empire's costs.
options.explanation: Sensible, but not what happened. Philip kept fighting, and in 1576 his unpaid soldiers sacked the city of Antwerp (the "Spanish Fury"), which turned even more of the Netherlands against Spain.

options.text: Borrow even more from foreign bankers, even at higher interest.
options.explanation: This is what Spain did again and again, and the debts only grew. Spain went bankrupt again in 1596, and interest payments ate up much of the silver.

options.text: Stop paying your soldiers entirely and let them live off the land in the Netherlands. The rebels' towns can feed them.

collapse.text: Furious, unpaid soldiers looted the cities they were supposed to protect. The Netherlands, your bankers, and finally your own nobles turned against you, and your empire broke apart.

options.explanation: In 1576 unpaid Spanish soldiers really did sack Antwerp, killing thousands, in the "Spanish Fury." It pushed more of the Netherlands into open rebellion, though Spain itself survived.

armada.title: The Spanish Armada
armada.text: Protestant England, under Queen Elizabeth I, has been helping the Dutch rebels, and English captains like Francis Drake raid your treasure ships. In 1587 England executed Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic. You have gathered a huge fleet, the Armada, to carry an army across the sea and invade England.

scene.title: The Armada fails
scene.caption: The Armada sails from Lisbon, but English fire ships and guns break it up off Calais and Gravelines. Storms wreck many ships as it limps home around Scotland and Ireland.

context.text: Your careful spending means the treasury can actually afford a war, if you choose one.

options.text: Call off the invasion. Guard your treasure fleets with warships, strengthen your ports against raiders like Drake, and seek peace with England instead of a risky war.
options.explanation: The wiser choice. Philip sent the Armada in 1588, and it was beaten by English fire ships and gunnery, then wrecked by storms off Scotland and Ireland. Spain stayed powerful, but its reputation took a heavy blow.

options.text: Send the Armada to invade England and restore Catholicism there.
options.explanation: This is what Philip did. English ships, fire ships, and storms destroyed much of the Armada in 1588, a famous defeat that cost Spain ships, sailors, and money.

options.text: Send the Armada, but only after building better long-range cannons and a clear plan to pick up your army in the Netherlands.
options.explanation: Better preparation might have helped, since the Armada's guns and its link-up with the army in the Netherlands were weak points. Still, invading England was a huge gamble, and in 1588 it failed.

moriscos.title: The Moriscos
moriscos.text: You are King Philip III. About 300,000 Moriscos live in Spain, many of them skilled farmers in Valencia and Aragon. Some Church leaders claim they secretly practice Islam and might help the Ottomans. They want the Moriscos expelled.

options.text: Let the Moriscos stay and keep farming. They are skilled, settled people, and loyalty can be earned.
options.explanation: The road not taken. Philip III expelled about 300,000 Moriscos between 1609 and 1614, which emptied farmland in Valencia and Aragon and added to Spain's decline in the 1600s.

options.text: Expel them all from Spain, as the Church leaders urge. If even a few secretly practice Islam and help the Ottomans, your coasts are in danger, and a fully Catholic Spain will be safer.
options.explanation: This is what Philip III did, starting in 1609. Losing so many skilled farmers and workers hurt the economy, especially in Valencia, as Spain began a long decline.

options.text: Force them to move to other parts of Spain, away from the coasts.
options.explanation: Something like this was tried after a Morisco revolt in Granada (1568–1571), and it didn't end the suspicion. Philip III expelled the Moriscos in 1609, damaging the economy.

decline.title: An Empire Coming Apart
decline.text: Spain is exhausted. Decades of war, including the Thirty Years' War, have drained the treasury, and silver shipments from the Americas are falling. Your chief minister, the Count-Duke of Olivares, has tried to make Catalonia and Portugal (ruled by Spain's king since 1580) pay more for the wars. In 1640, both rise in revolt.

options.text: Make peace in Europe, compromise with Catalonia, and accept that Portugal may go.
options.explanation: Realistic. Spain made peace with the Dutch (1648) and France (1659), won back Catalonia in 1652, and recognized Portugal's independence in 1668. Spain survived as a major empire, but no longer as Europe's leading power.

options.text: Refuse any compromise: raise crushing new taxes everywhere, keep fighting France, and send armies against Portugal and Catalonia at once. Weakness invites revolt.

collapse.text: Fighting France, Portugal, and Catalonia at the same time bankrupted the Crown. Armies went unpaid, provinces broke away, and the Spanish Empire fell apart.

options.explanation: Too much at once. Spain really did fight on all three fronts and went bankrupt again in 1647, but it put Catalonia first (recovering it in 1652) and finally accepted Portugal's independence in 1668. Crushing new taxes on top of that could have set off revolts everywhere.

options.text: Raise taxes on Castile yet again to pay for everything. It is the heart of the empire and has carried its wars before, and squeezing loyal Castile is safer than giving in to rebels.
options.explanation: Castile, the heart of the empire, was already crushed by taxes, and its population and economy were shrinking. Spain survived by making peace with its enemies over the next decades.
